lesson.title: Is the Slope Real, or Just Noise?
lesson.summary: The t-test for the slope determines whether an observed sample slope is statistically distinguishable from a population slope of zero, using the test statistic t = (b1 - 0)/SE(b1) with n-2 degrees of freedom.
lesson.body:
Every slope you compute from a sample, call it b1, is only an estimate of some true population slope, call it β1. Even if the real relationship between x and y in the population has β1 exactly equal to 0, meaning no linear relationship at all, a random sample of data will almost never produce a sample slope of exactly 0. Random sampling variability guarantees some wobble. The question a t-test for the slope answers is: is the b1 we calculated far enough from 0 that it's implausible to have happened just from that wobble, or is it small enough that a true population slope of 0 remains a perfectly believable explanation for what we saw?

This is the same logic as the one-sample t-test for a mean, just aimed at a different statistic. We set up H0: β1 = 0 (no linear relationship in the population) against Ha: β1 ≠ 0 (or a one-directional alternative if the context calls for it), then compute a test statistic of the same basic shape as before: (statistic minus hypothesized value) divided by standard error. Here that's t = (b1 − 0) / SE(b1), and we compare it to a t-distribution with df = n − 2. The 2 gets subtracted because fitting a line uses up two pieces of information from the data, the intercept and the slope, before there's anything left over to estimate how much residual scatter remains.

Here is a small worked example, small enough to check every step by hand. Six students report how many hours they studied for a quiz (x) and their resulting score out of 20 (y): (1, 8), (2, 10), (3, 11), (4, 14), (5, 15), (6, 17). The mean of x is 3.5 and the mean of y is 12.5. Using the least-squares formulas, the slope works out to b1 = 1.8 and the intercept to b0 = 6.2, so the fitted line is predicted score = 6.2 + 1.8 × hours studied.

The standard error of this slope (derived carefully in the next chapter) turns out to be SE(b1) ≈ 0.1069. That gives t = 1.8 / 0.1069 ≈ 16.84, with df = 6 − 2 = 4. A t-statistic that large, on 4 degrees of freedom, is far out in the tail: the p-value is well below 0.0001. Since that p-value is tiny compared to any reasonable significance level like 0.05, we reject H0. There is strong evidence of a real, positive linear relationship between hours studied and quiz score for the population these six students represent.

Two cautions to carry forward. First, this tiny sample of six was chosen purely so every number here could be verified by hand; a real study would want far more data before drawing conclusions. Second, and more importantly, rejecting H0 only tells us the relationship is very unlikely to be pure chance, it says nothing yet about whether the relationship is big enough to matter, or whether studying actually causes the higher scores rather than just being associated with them. Those are separate questions, tackled in later chapters.
